turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How often should I pump up my bike tires?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For a road bike, about once a week. Thinner tires lose air faster than you'd think.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And how do I know the right pressure?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's printed on the side of the tire as a range. Aim somewhere in the middle for everyday riding.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've just been squeezing them / and guessing, honestly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A lot of people do. A floor pump with a gauge takes the guessing out and isn't expensive.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I go lower if it's raining?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A little lower, yes. It gives you more grip on wet roads.

turns.text: My chain makes this squeaking noise every time I pedal.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That usually means it's dry. A bit of chain lube should fix it.

turns.text: Can I just use cooking oil?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I wouldn't. It gets sticky and collects dirt. Proper bike lube is cheap and lasts a long time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. How do I put it on?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Put one drop on each link while you slowly turn the pedals backward. Then wipe off the extra with a rag.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I clean it first, or / is that overkill?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If it looks black and gritty, wipe it down first. Otherwise you're just mixing new oil with old dirt.

turns.text: Is it a bad idea to bike in the winter?

turns.text: Not at all, lots of people do. You just need good lights, warm gloves and a bit more caution on ice.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try lobster style gloves, they keep fingers together for warmth but still let you brake easily.

turns.speaker: user

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a sensible compromise. Ride on dry days and skip the icy ones.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I need special tires for the cold days?

turns.speaker: moshi

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I make sure my bike seat is the right height?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sit on the bike with your heel on the pedal at the bottom of the stroke. Your leg should be almost straight.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And when I pedal normally?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then, with the ball of your foot on the pedal, you'll have a slight bend in the knee. That's the sweet spot.

turns.text: Mine feels kind of low, / my knees come up high.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's very common, and it's tiring for your legs. Raise it a couple of centimeters at a time and test ride each change.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Will I still reach the ground?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Probably only on tiptoes, and that's normal. When you stop, slide forward off the saddle.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's the safest way to ride past parked cars?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Stay about a car door's width away from them. That way, if someone opens a door suddenly, you won't hit it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: But then cars behind me get annoyed.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They might, but your safety matters more. Riding confidently in the lane makes you more visible too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about at junctions?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try to make eye contact with drivers and avoid riding up the inside of big vehicles, especially lorries turning left.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's terrifying.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's good to know though. Most rides are completely uneventful, these habits just keep it that way.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I fix a slipping chain? It keeps jumping when I change gears.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Often the gear cable just needs a small adjustment. Look for a little barrel adjuster where the cable enters the rear derailleur.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, the little round thing?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's it. Turn it a quarter turn at a time while you change gears, until the shifting feels smooth.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Which way do I turn it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If the chain is slow to move to bigger cogs, turn it anticlockwise. If it's slow to drop to smaller ones, clockwise.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, and if that / doesn't fix it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it could be a worn chain or a bent derailleur hanger. That's a quick job for a bike shop.

turns.text: Set a reminder, or take a sip every time you reach a hilltop or a junction.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I bring food too?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, for anything over ninety minutes. Bananas, cereal bars, or even a small sandwich.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Honestly I thought I could just / power through on breakfast.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A lot of people try that and run out of energy halfway. It's called bonking, and it's not fun.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it okay to ride on the pavement with my kids?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It depends on local rules. In many places young kids are allowed, but adults are expected to ride on the road.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: But I'm not leaving my seven year old on the pavement alone.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Totally fair. Lots of parents walk their bike next to the child, or use quiet residential streets and cycle paths.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Are there any cycle paths near parks / usually?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Often, yes. Check the local council's cycling map, they usually show the family friendly routes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good idea. My son loves the park.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then plan a loop around it. Kids enjoy having a destination, like the playground or a duck pond.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to ride a century one day. Is that just a hundred miles?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly, a hundred miles in one ride. Some people also do a metric century, which is a hundred kilometers.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long would that take me?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: At an average of fifteen miles an hour, about seven hours of riding, plus stops.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Wow. That's a whole day.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is. Most people start early, plan a couple of cafe stops, and finish by late afternoon.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe I'll start / with the metric one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Great first goal. It's a big achievement on its own and builds you up for the full hundred.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I train for it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Build up your longest ride gradually, add about ten percent each week, and include an easy week every month.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to start riding but I'm honestly terrified of traffic.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a really common fear. Many people start on quiet routes, like parks and cycle paths, and build confidence from there.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about my commute?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try riding it on a Sunday morning first, when it's quiet, so you learn the route without stress.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's actually a great idea.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some cities also offer free cycling lessons for adults. They teach you how to position yourself in traffic.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh really? I'd do that.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look up your local council's website. And remember, you can always get off and walk a tricky junction.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What does bike fitting mean? A friend said I need one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's when a specialist adjusts your bike to your body, saddle height, handlebar reach, cleat position and so on.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it worth it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If you ride a lot and get aches in your knees, back or hands, it can make a big difference.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My neck hurts after long rides.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That can mean your handlebars are too far away or too low. A fitter would probably raise them or shorten the stem.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is that expensive / or just like a quick check?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A full fit can cost about as much as a nice pair of shoes. A basic adjustment at a bike shop is much cheaper.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I carry groceries on my bike?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A rear rack with panniers is the classic setup. They clip on and hold a surprising amount.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about a basket?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A front basket is handy for small things, but heavy loads up front can make steering wobbly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I usually do / one big weekly shop.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then two panniers or a bike trailer would be best. Trailers can carry a lot, even a crate of drinks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is a backpack bad?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fine for light stuff, but heavy bags make your back sweaty and sore. Let the bike carry the weight.

option_sets.lead_in: I need a new bike and I've narrowed it down, but I'm stuck.
options: The first one is a light road bike, really fast, but it has thin tires and no rack.
Then there's a hybrid with wider tires, a rack on the back and a more upright seat.
And the last one is an electric bike, heavy and pricey, but hills would be no problem at all.
moshi_comment: It depends on what you'll use it for. The road bike is great for fitness rides but awkward for carrying groceries, while the hybrid handles commuting and errands easily. The electric bike makes sense if your route is hilly and you don't want to arrive sweaty.
The hybrid sounds like the best all rounder of the three. How long and how hilly is your usual ride? If it's steep, the electric bike might be worth the price.

option_sets.lead_in: We're planning a cycling day trip and I can't decide on the route.
options: One route follows the coast, about thirty miles, flat, with a nice cafe at the end.
Another one goes up through the vineyards, shorter, but with two pretty steep climbs.
The third is a forest trail, mostly gravel, quiet and shady, maybe twenty miles.
moshi_comment: The coast route is the easiest and the cafe makes a great finish. The vineyard route has the best views, but those climbs could wear out a mixed group. The forest trail is lovely on a hot day, as long as everyone's bike can handle gravel.
I'd pick the coast unless your group loves hills. Are all of you on road bikes? If so, I'd skip the gravel forest trail.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm planning my route for a weekend bikepacking trip and there are three loops I like.
options: A coastal loop, about sixty miles, with a campsite right by the beach and a pub nearby.
There's also a hill loop that's shorter, around forty miles, but with a big climb and an amazing wild camping spot.
Or a river valley route, flat and gentle, with a few villages and a farm campsite with hot showers.
moshi_comment: The river valley is the easiest and the hot showers are a real luxury on a bikepacking trip. The coast loop is the best all rounder, with a beach camp and a pub dinner. The hill loop is for when you want a challenge and real solitude.

If it's your first bikepacking trip, I'd pick the river valley, it lets you learn how the loaded bike handles without big climbs. The hill loop is great once you're confident. How heavy is your setup?

option_sets.lead_in: I need a new helmet and I've got it down to a few options.
options: One is a basic commuter helmet, cheap and comfy, with a built in rear light.
Another is a lightweight road helmet with loads of vents, but no light and quite pricey.
There's also a folding helmet that collapses flat to fit in my bag.
Or a full face mountain bike helmet my brother is giving away for free.
moshi_comment: For daily commuting, the basic helmet with a built in light is really practical. The road helmet only makes sense for long, hot rides. The folding one is great if you use bike share and carry it around.
Skip the full face, it's overkill for town and hot on a commute. Do you ride your own bike or use bike share? If it's bike share, the folding helmet is a winner.

option_sets.lead_in: My work is offering a cycle to work scheme and I've got three bikes on my shortlist.
options: There's a gravel bike that can handle roads and dirt tracks, with space for mudguards.
Then a lightweight carbon road bike, really quick, but it eats most of the budget.
Or a sturdy electric hybrid with a big battery and built in lights.
moshi_comment: For commuting plus weekend fun, the gravel bike is the most versatile, and mudguards make rainy days easy. The carbon road bike is fast, but less practical day to day. The e-hybrid is great if your commute is long or hilly.
I'd lean toward the gravel bike unless your commute is really long. How far is your ride to work? If it's over ten miles, the electric hybrid could change everything.
